newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Sticken Mir crew stands down, says worst over.
newsitem.headline: Sticken Mir crew stands down, says worst over.

text.p: Russian space officials decided on Monday to stand down the weary and accident-prone cosmonauts on board their crippled Mir space station and leave risky repairs to a relief crew due to fly next month.
Commander Vasily Tsibliyev, who developed heart trouble, and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin will keep Mir ticking over in orbit until they hand over to replacements in about two weeks.

Mission director Vladimir Solovyov told reporters at Mission Control outside Moscow that ground experts took the decision because more equipment was needed and the relief team of commander Anatoly Solovyov and engineer Pavel Vinogradov would be fresher.

Solovyov's deputy, Sergei Krikalyov, told Ekho Moskvy radio one of their tasks will not be easy -- trying to re-seal the Spektr module that was holed in a collision with a cargo craft on June 25 in Mir's worst accident in 11 years in orbit.
"It is still unclear where the leak is and whether it is possible to restore the module," Krikalyov said, adding that the new crew would have to try "several options".

The pair will don spacesuits to enter the airless Spektr and reconnect power cables from its solar panels around August 18-20. They are also in training for a spacewalk outside the complex in late August or early September to inspect the hole punched in it during last month's collision.

The job of reconnecting the cables had been planned for this week until one of the three tired men on board pulled out the wrong plug on Thursday and crashed the on-board computer, sending Mir tumbling through space and its electricity supply, already on half-power, down to the minimum.

Vladimir Solovyov, no relation to the new Mir commander, said he was confident the world's only orbital laboratory would now be patched up. "I think we will be able to revive Spektr and get Mir to continue its normal work," he said.
There were no plans to delay September's next NASA Shuttle mission bringing up U.S. navy commander Wendy Lawrence, 37, to replace NASA physicist Michael Foale.

Veteran shuttle commander Frank Culbertson, who oversees NASA's missions to Mir, told reporters on Monday at Cape Canaveral the Russian space authorities had tentatively scheduled the repair work for August 20.
A spacewalk to inspect the outside of the damaged module was scheduled for September 3.

The U.S. space agency was considering delivering additional repair equipment to Mir in September aboard the Shuttle Atlantis, icluding a cutting tool to remove Spektr's damaged solar panel and instruments to locate the module's hull breach.

Russian officials, who rely on Mir's foreign income to keep the post-Soviet space programme going, have asked NASA to consider flying the Shuttle around Mir to zoom its hi-definition cameras in on the damage.

British-born Foale, 40, who stepped forward to replace Tsibliyev on the original repair team when the commander developed an irregular heart beat a week ago, will help out the relief crew but will play no active part in their spacewalks.
The scientist's experiments on Mir since May have been disrupted by the loss of power following the collision.
After several more weeks in the stuffy, grubby gloom of the station, he will return to Earth after the Shuttle docks on September 20, leaving Lawrence for her four-month tour of duty.
A Soyuz spacecraft with commander Solovyov and engineer Vinogradov will blast off from Baikonur cosmodrome on August 5.
They will leave behind Frenchman Leopold Eyharts whose three-week scientific mission is now likely to go ahead in January, after Mir is back in working order.
Tsibliyev and Lazutkin will fly home aboard a Soyuz two weeks ahead of schedule on August 14.
